readerTitle: The test was winning. That was the problem.
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Optimizely의 2015년 통계 방식 변경) + 실제 연구 (Armitage 외 1969, 반복 검정) + 가상 적용 (보험사 고객지원팀, 호텔 레스토랑)
insight: 결과를 보는 것은 괜찮다. 문제는 결과를 보고 나서 언제 멈출지 정하는 것이다. 종료 시점은 시작 전에 정해야 한다.
misconception: 테스트 중간에 '유의미한' 차이가 보이면 그 결과는 믿을 수 있으니 바로 멈추고 적용해도 된다.

sources.text: Armitage, P., McPherson, C. K., & Rowe, B. C. (1969). Repeated Significance Tests on Accumulating Data. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A, 132(2), 235–244.
Johari, R., Pekelis, L., Walsh, D. et al. (2017). Peeking at A/B Tests: Why it matters, and what to do about it. KDD 2017.
Miller, E. (2010). How Not To Run an A/B Test (blog post)
보험사 고객지원팀, 호텔 레스토랑 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 차트 수치(1회 확인 5%, 2회 약 8%, 5회 약 14%, 10회 약 19%)는 Armitage 외(1969)의 반복 유의성 검정 표(정규분포, 양측 5%, 동일 간격 확인)를 기억에 근거해 반올림한 값입니다. 게시 전 원문 표와 대조하세요.

Optimizely가 2015년 Stats Engine을 출시하며 고객들이 결과를 계속 확인하고 일찍 멈추는 관행(peeking)을 주요 이유로 들었다는 점을 Optimizely 발표 자료와 Johari 외(2017)로 확인하세요. 카드에는 '수천 개 기업' 같은 구체적 수치는 쓰지 않았고 'thousands of companies ran online tests'는 업계 전반에 대한 일반적 서술입니다.
5번 카드의 '+12%가 나중에 +3%'는 설명용 예시이며 특정 연구 수치가 아닙니다. 문장에서도 'say'로 가정임을 드러냈습니다.
임상시험의 중간 분석 규칙(사전에 정한 조기 중단 기준, 초기 확인 시 더 엄격한 기준)은 일반적인 설명입니다. 특정 시험 사례는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The test was winning. That was the problem.
body: By the early 2010s, many companies ran online tests with tools that showed live results. Teams watched the numbers daily and stopped the moment a new version looked like a winner.
In 2015, the testing company Optimizely rebuilt how its tool calculated results. A key reason: that habit of stopping early was producing "winners" that weren't real.

image.label: A team cheering at a live dashboard that shows a green winner badge
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실에서 몇 명이 모니터 앞에서 환호하고, 화면에는 초록색 'Winner!' 배지와 들쭉날쭉한 실시간 그래프. 그래프 끝부분은 흐릿하게 처리해 아직 끝나지 않았다는 느낌. 실제 회사 로고나 제품 화면은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Four days in, the new version is ahead.
body: You lead the support team inside a large insurance company. You're testing a new email reply template against the old one. The plan: four weeks, then compare customer ratings.
After four days, the new template is clearly ahead. Your director says the gap is already "statistically significant" and wants it rolled out to everyone on Monday.

options.text: Roll it out Monday. The result is significant
options.feedback: You gain three weeks, but a significant result at an early look is far less trustworthy than it sounds. Four days may have caught a lucky stretch.

options.text: Finish the four weeks, then decide
options.feedback: You may wait a few weeks for a better template, but you get the answer the test was designed to give.

options.text: Check daily and roll out once it has stayed ahead for a week
options.feedback: Safer than stopping on day four. But it's a stopping rule invented mid-test, and every daily check is another chance to be fooled.

cards.title: Every look is another roll of the dice.
body: A standard test accepts a 5% chance of a false winner, but only if you check once, at the end. Statisticians showed in 1969 that checking along the way and stopping at the first significant result raises that chance with every look.

groups.label: Chance of declaring a winner when there is no real difference

cards.callout: Nothing about the test changed. Only how often someone looked, and when they stopped.

cards.title: Stopping a test too early
body: **Stopping too early** means ending a test when the results look good, instead of at a point you chose before it started.

The trap is subtle. Looking isn't the problem. Deciding when to stop *based on what you see* is. Results drift up and down by chance. If you stop the moment they drift your way, you turn a random swing into a decision.
cards.softwareNote: Many A/B testing tools now offer sequential statistics, methods built to stay accurate even when you check often. If yours doesn't, set the sample size before launch and ignore the live significance badge until you reach it.

cards.title: Early winners tend to shrink.
body: Early in a test, a handful of unusual customers can swing the totals. A big early lead is often part real effect, part luck.
Stop at a high point and you lock in the luck. When the change goes to everyone, the luck doesn't come along. Say the test showed +12%; months later the real gain looks closer to +3%.
It cuts both ways. Teams also kill good ideas that simply started slow.

image.label: A line that swings wildly early, then settles near a small gain
image.brief: 선 그래프 인포그래픽. 가로축 'Days', 세로축 'Lift'. 초반에 선이 크게 위아래로 흔들리다가 점점 작은 양수 값 근처로 수렴. 초반 최고점에 빨간 점과 'Stopped here: +12%' 라벨, 끝부분에 'Real effect: +3%' 라벨.

cards.title: Sometimes stopping early is right.
body: Medical trials do stop early, for example when a treatment causes harm. But they set those stopping rules before the trial begins, and they demand stronger evidence at each early look.

In business, stop at once if a change is hurting customers or breaking something. Waiting has a cost too; a test that never ends helps no one. The fix isn't endless patience. It's **choosing the length, or the stopping rule, before you start**.

cards.title: Now it's a hotel restaurant.
body: You run the restaurant in a city hotel. You're testing a new set lunch menu against the regular one, alternating weeks for eight weeks.
After two weeks, average spend per table on the new menu is 10% lower. Your chef wants to stop and drop it.

options.text: Stop now. Two weeks of lower sales is enough
options.feedback: You save six weeks but make the same mistake in reverse. A slow start can be noise, and you might kill a menu that would have won.

options.text: Run all eight weeks, unless guests complain or food costs spike
options.feedback: The test stays honest, and you still have an exit for real harm, one you set by a rule rather than by the score.

options.text: Stop, rework the menu, and start a fresh eight-week test
options.feedback: A clean restart is honest, but you throw away two weeks of data and may be reacting to noise, not a real problem.

cards.title: Decide when a test ends before it begins.
body: Write down how long a test runs, or how many customers it needs, before launch. Then let it finish, unless something is clearly causing harm.
**Try it today:** for any test or trial you're running, note the end date and what result would change your mind. Share it so no one can quietly move the finish line.
